harmonicFunction: Am (i) - Tonic minor, the home key and emotional center of the piece
G (VII) - Subtonic major, creates descending stepwise bass motion from Am
Em (v) - Minor dominant, weaker resolution than the V7 but maintains minor character
Dm (iv) - Subdominant, adds depth and pathos in the classical tradition
E7 (V7) - Dominant seventh, provides the strong classical cadence resolution to Am
C (III) - Relative major, used for brightness in Theme B
F (VI) - Submediant, warm harmonic color in the middle sections
Bdim (ii dim) - Diminished chord adding classical tension in the development

techniques.name: Classical Fingerpicking (PIMA)
techniques.description: Full classical right-hand technique using the thumb (p), index (i), middle (m), and ring (a) fingers independently to play bass, harmony, and melody simultaneously

notes: p (pulgar/thumb) plays bass notes on strings 6, 5, and 4
i (indice/index) plays string 3
m (medio/middle) plays string 2
a (anular/ring) plays string 1
All four fingers must operate independently and simultaneously
The thumb often provides a steady bass line while fingers play melody above it
sequence: Practice free stroke (tirando) on each string with each assigned finger
Develop thumb independence by playing a bass note pattern while holding chord shapes
Add single melody notes on the high strings while the thumb keeps the bass going
Gradually combine bass, harmony, and melody into full three-voice texture
Apply to the Theme A passage where bass walks down A-G-F#-F-E
tips: Keep fingernails on the picking hand trimmed to a consistent length for tone
Sit in proper classical position with the guitar supported on the left leg
The wrist should be arched so fingers approach strings at a perpendicular angle
Start incredibly slowly - independence between thumb and fingers takes months
Practice each voice (bass, melody) separately before combining them
details.progression: Am - G - Em - Am - Dm - E7 - Am (Theme A)

techniques.name: Rapid Position Shifts
techniques.description: The piece requires the fretting hand to move rapidly between different positions on the neck, from open position to the 7th, 10th, and even 12th positions within a few beats

notes: Theme A operates primarily in open position (frets 0-3)
Development section moves to 5th and 7th positions
Climactic passages reach the 10th and 12th positions
Position shifts must be executed cleanly without audible gaps
The thumb behind the neck must reposition smoothly during shifts
sequence: Map out every position shift in the piece and mark them in your score
Practice each shift in isolation: play the last note before the shift, then the first note after
Use guide fingers (a finger that stays on the same string during the shift) when possible
Practice the shift gradually faster until it can be executed at tempo
Focus on landing accurately on the target fret every time
tips: Look ahead in the music mentally - know where you are going before you move
Keep the thumb behind the neck relaxed so it can slide freely during shifts
Practice shifts with your eyes closed to develop positional muscle memory
A slight portamento (slide) during shifts is acceptable and can sound musical
Mark difficult shifts in your sheet music so you remember to prepare for them

techniques.name: Bass-Melody Independence
techniques.description: Playing two independent musical lines simultaneously: a walking or rhythmic bass line with the thumb and a melodic line with the fingers, essentially making the guitar sound like two instruments

notes: The bass line often has its own rhythmic and melodic identity separate from the melody
In Theme A, the bass walks down chromatically (A-G-F#-F-E) while the melody moves independently above
This two-voice texture is the foundation of classical guitar repertoire
Each voice should have its own dynamic and tonal character
The bass provides harmonic foundation while the melody carries the tune
sequence: Learn the bass line alone, playing only the thumb part through each section
Learn the melody alone, playing only the finger part through each section
Combine them very slowly, one measure at a time
Practice the combined texture at 50% tempo until it feels secure
Gradually increase tempo while maintaining the independence of each voice
tips: Think of yourself as a two-person ensemble: bass player and melody player
The bass notes should sustain while the melody moves above - use proper left-hand fingering
If one voice starts to suffer, slow down and isolate the problematic passage
Listen to recordings of classical guitarists (Julian Bream, John Williams) for reference
This skill develops over months and years - be patient with the process
details.progression: Am - G - Em - Am (Theme A with walking bass)

sections.name: Intro / Theme A
sections.description: The famous opening theme with the descending bass line (A-G-F#-F-E) under an arpeggiated melody, establishing the piece's dramatic classical character
sections.progression: Am - G - Em - Am - Dm - E7 - Am
notes: The most recognizable passage - the descending bass line defines the piece
Thumb maintains the walking bass while fingers play arpeggiated chords above
Keep the bass notes ringing by holding chord shapes with the fretting hand
The tempo builds gradually from the opening - start slower and accelerate slightly

sections.name: Theme B
sections.description: Contrasting brighter theme moving to the C major key area, featuring faster arpeggio patterns and a more optimistic melodic character
sections.progression: C - G - Am - F - G - C
notes: Shift to the relative major key (C) for brightness and contrast
Faster finger movements with more rapid arpeggio patterns
The melody is in the high voice while bass provides harmonic grounding
This section showcases the folk-influenced side of the composition

sections.name: Development
sections.description: The most harmonically adventurous section, exploring circle-of-fifths movements, diminished chords, and rapid position shifts across the fretboard
sections.progression: Am - Dm - G - C - F - Bdim - E7 - Am
notes: The most technically demanding section with rapid position changes
Circle-of-fifths harmonic movement provides classical sophistication
The diminished chord (Bdim) adds dramatic tension before the V7-i cadence
Position shifts move the hand from open position up to the 7th-10th fret area

sections.name: Theme A Reprise
sections.description: Return of the opening theme with slight variations and added ornamentation, bringing the piece back to familiar territory after the development
sections.progression: Am - G - Em - Am - Dm - E7 - Am
notes: Same harmonic structure as the opening but with added embellishments
Slight variations in the melody add freshness to the repeated theme
The bass line is identical to the opening for structural unity
Ornamentation can include hammer-ons, pull-offs, and grace notes

sections.name: Coda
sections.description: The climactic final section building to the piece's highest point of intensity with rapid scale runs and powerful chordal strumming before resolving to a final Am chord
notes: The most intense passage with rapid scalar runs up and down the fretboard
Builds to the dynamic peak of the entire piece
Strummed chords may replace fingerpicking for the climactic moments
The final V7-i cadence (E7 to Am) provides a definitive classical resolution

alternatives: Steel-string acoustic guitar (changes the character but still playable)
Parlor-sized acoustic for a smaller-bodied option
guitar.pickup: None needed - this is an acoustic/classical piece (optional pickup for live amplification)

alternatives: AER Compact 60 (for amplified classical guitar performance)
Direct PA via quality acoustic DI

effects.reverb: Natural room acoustics preferred; light hall reverb if performing in a dry space
effects.other: None - the beauty of the piece comes from the natural guitar tone

beginner.focus: Develop basic classical fingerpicking technique and learn a simplified version of Theme A
steps: Learn proper classical guitar hand position (both hands)
Practice PIMA finger assignments on open strings until comfortable
Learn the Am, G, Em, Dm, and E7 chord shapes used in Theme A
Play a simplified version of Theme A with just the bass notes and basic arpeggios

intermediate.focus: Learn the full Theme A and Theme B with proper bass-melody independence
steps: Learn the complete Theme A with the walking bass line and melody combined
Practice Theme B in C major with the faster arpeggio patterns
Work on bass-melody independence: isolate each voice then combine
Build position-shifting technique for the passages that leave open position

advanced.focus: Master all sections including the Development and Coda, perform the complete piece
steps: Learn the harmonically complex Development section with all position shifts
Master the virtuosic Coda with rapid scale runs and climactic chords
Memorize the complete piece and work on musical expression and dynamics
Record yourself and refine interpretation by comparing to professional recordings

commonMistakes: Trying to play at tempo too soon - this piece requires extremely slow practice for months
Neglecting the bass line independence and letting it blur into the melody
Tension in the fretting hand and wrist during position shifts, causing fatigue and missed notes
Playing all notes at the same volume instead of bringing out the melody over the accompaniment
practiceRoutine: Warm up with PIMA exercises on open strings for 5 minutes, focusing on finger independence
Practice one section at a time at 50% tempo: Theme A one day, Theme B the next
Isolate position shifts: play the 4 notes before and after each shift 20 times
Work on bass-melody separation: play bass only, then melody only, then combine slowly
focusAreas: Classical right-hand technique with proper PIMA finger assignment and independence
Clean position shifts across the fretboard without gaps or buzzing
Simultaneous bass and melody lines with distinct dynamic levels for each voice
Musical phrasing and dynamic shaping across the A-B-Development-A-Coda form
metronomeWork: Practice Theme A at 72 BPM (half tempo) until every note is clean and the bass is independent
Gradually build tempo in 10 BPM increments, spending at least 3 days at each tempo
Practice the Development section position shifts with a metronome at 60 BPM
Target full performance tempo of 144 BPM only after all sections are secure at 120 BPM
